intro: San Diego's trees were planted, not inherited. In 1892 the city leased Kate Sessions park land on condition she plant a hundred trees a year in Balboa Park, and the 1915 exposition brought in much of the rest. The oldest anyone can date here is around 130 years, genuinely old for this city. All six are free: two Moreton Bay figs, a cypress from an island off Baja, a kauri from New Zealand, a tipu that outlived its nursery, and a low tangle of tea tree Sessions likely planted herself.
meta_description: San Diego planted its own shade. A 1914 Moreton Bay fig 12 metres round, a Guadalupe cypress from 1892, and a New Zealand kauri on the Plaza.
question_answer: The oldest tree in San Diego is a Guadalupe Island cypress on the Sixth Avenue side of Balboa Park, beside the chess and horseshoe club building, at roughly 130 years. San Diego Magazine went looking for the city's oldest tree in 2020 and named this one, putting it at about 128 years then. It is one of the trees Kate Sessions planted under her 1892 lease of park land at Sixth and Upas, which obliged her to plant a hundred trees a year in Balboa Park.
question_meta: San Diego's oldest tree is a Guadalupe Island cypress in Balboa Park, planted around 1892 by Kate Sessions and now roughly 130 years old.
question_context:
A hundred and thirty years is a young answer by the standards of most cities, and here it is the right one. San Diego's shade is not old growth that a city grew up around; it was planted, mostly between 1892 and the 1915 Panama-California Exposition, and a tree that predates that effort is hard to find on the mesa. So the oldest trees in the city are the earliest plantings rather than the last survivors of anything.

The cypress has a second thing going for it. Cupressus guadalupensis grows wild in one place on earth, Isla Guadalupe off Baja California, where feral goats have long been the main threat to it, and a large mainland specimen is unusual for that reason alone. Nobody has published a girth or a height for this one, which is the frustrating part of a tree that two independent sources both call enormously tall.

The runner-up is easier to date exactly. The Moreton Bay fig outside the Natural History Museum went in as a five-gallon sapling in 1914 and is the last plant left from the county garden exhibit it was planted for.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in San Diego?
faq.a: A Guadalupe Island cypress on the Sixth Avenue edge of Balboa Park, roughly 130 years old, planted by Kate Sessions under her 1892 lease of park land. San Diego Magazine put it at about 128 years when it went looking for the city's oldest tree in 2020.

faq.q: Why are San Diego's oldest trees only a century old?
faq.a: Because the city planted them. Kate Sessions began putting a hundred trees a year into Balboa Park from 1892, and the 1915 Panama-California Exposition brought in much of the rest. A tree here that has stood since the 1890s has been there almost as long as the park has.

faq.q: Are San Diego's remarkable trees free to visit?
faq.a: All six are. Five stand in Balboa Park with no ticket and no gate, though Marston House itself charges for tours inside; the sixth is on a street corner in Pacific Beach beside its historical landmark plaque. Museum admission is only needed for the galleries, never for the trees outside them.

faq.q: What are the two newest trees added to this page?
faq.a: The Twisted Tea Tree at Marston House, a low tangle of Australian tea tree likely planted around 1906 by Kate Sessions herself, and a second Moreton Bay fig over Palm Canyon, planted in the 1930s, whose buttress roots pour over the canyon edge like a set of flying buttresses.

faq.q: Did Kate Sessions plant the big fig in Balboa Park?
faq.a: Probably not, and nobody can show that she did. The Natural History Museum, which the fig stands outside, says openly that the attribution to Sessions has no documentation behind it. The tipu tree in Pacific Beach is the one on this list she is independently credited with planting.

trees.name: The Moreton Bay Fig of Balboa Park

location.address: North entrance plaza, San Diego Natural History Museum, Balboa Park, San Diego, CA

trees.story:
This fig went into the ground as a five-gallon sapling. That was 1914, planted for the San Diego County garden exhibit at the Panama-California Exposition the year after, and it is the last plant from that exhibit still alive. A survey for the California Registry of Big Trees in 1996 put it at 24 metres tall with a crown 37 metres across and a trunk 12.3 metres round, though that last figure is a buttressed fig mass rather than one clean stem. Moreton Bay figs do not so much grow a trunk as accumulate one.

Its worst years came from being admired. Decades of visitors walking the ground under the crown compacted the soil and damaged the surface roots, and by the 1980s the tree was going backwards. In 1989 it was trimmed and the ground beneath it fenced off. It recovered. The aerial roots now hanging from the limbs are the sign of a fig doing well rather than merely holding on.

Some accounts credit the planting to Kate Sessions, who supplied a great deal of what grows in this park. The Natural History Museum, whose north entrance the tree stands outside, says flatly that there is no documentation for that. A hundred and twelve years on, nobody knows whose hands put it in.

The measurements above are thirty years old. The tree has not stopped growing since.
trees.access: Free, in the open park outside the Natural History Museum. The ground beneath its crown has been fenced off since 1989 to protect the tree's surface roots from foot traffic, but the tree itself is fully visible from the plaza.
trees.transport: Served by MTS bus route 7 to Balboa Park (Park Blvd pedestrian overpass stop), about a 10 minute walk to the museum plaza.
trees.notes: Age counted from the 1914 planting, not from the exposition's 1915 opening. Girth is a buttressed fig mass, not a round trunk; do not restate it as a diameter. The Natural History Museum's own page explicitly says the Kate Sessions attribution has no documentation, so the story says so rather than repeating it. Flagged only because the registry measurements date from 1996.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by a buttressed, accumulated trunk mass 12.3 metres round and aerial roots hanging from the limbs. It stands outside the north entrance of the San Diego Natural History Museum, Balboa Park.

trees.name: The Kate Sessions Tipu Tree
trees.age_estimate: about a century old, planted in the 1920s

location.address: Northwest corner of Garnet Avenue and Pico Street, Pacific Beach, San Diego, CA (California Historical Landmark No. 764)

trees.story:
This tipu is the last living thing from Kate Sessions' final nursery. Sessions, the horticulturist San Diego calls the mother of Balboa Park, bought seven acres at Garnet and Pico in Pacific Beach in the 1920s, one source dating the purchase to 1924, and ran Soledad Terrace on the land. The nursery is gone. The tree is what is left of it.

She planted it in 1928 according to katestrees.org, a site kept by a researcher of her work, which also records it as a protected heritage tree. The California Historical Landmarks record gives the looser 'planted in the 1920s', which agrees. Nobody has published a girth or a height for it, so if you happen to be carrying a tape measure, we would like the number.

The bronze plaque beside it is California Historical Landmark No. 764, dedicated in 1961. Read it carefully, because it commemorates the nursery site and Sessions herself rather than this tree. The distinction matters here: her name gets attached to a great many San Diego trees without any document behind it, and this one is the exception, independently credited to her by several sources.

Tipuana tipu comes from Bolivia and Argentina. In early summer it drops sprays of yellow-orange flowers over whatever is underneath, which here is a street corner.
trees.how_to_recognise: It grows beside the bronze California Historical Landmark plaque on the northwest corner of Garnet Avenue and Pico Street.
verified_sources: https://californiahistoricallandmarks.wordpress.com/2013/03/15/no-764-kate-olivia-sessions-nursery-site/ (places the tipu tree closer to the corner than the marker, on the same NW corner; state landmark directions at https://ohp.parks.ca.gov/ListedResources/Detail/764)
trees.access: Free, on a public street corner. The tree and its California Historical Landmark plaque stand in the open on the northwest corner of Garnet Avenue and Pico Street.
trees.transport: Served by MTS bus routes through Pacific Beach on Garnet Avenue; roughly a 10 minute walk from the Mission Bay Dr / Garnet Ave corridor.
trees.notes: A directly documented Sessions planting, unlike the Balboa Park fig: several sources independently name her as the planter of this specific tree. Landmark coordinates mark the plaque at the corner rather than the tree, hence approximate precision. No girth or height found in any source checked.

best_time.label: late May and June, when the crown turns yellow-orange and then drops the lot onto the pavement

location_site.name: Northwest corner of Garnet Avenue and Pico Street (Kate Sessions Nursery site marker)

trees.name: The Guadalupe Island Cypress by the Horseshoe Club

location.address: By the San Diego Chess Club and Horseshoe Club building, 2225 6th Avenue, Balboa Park, San Diego, CA (Sixth Avenue near Ivy Street)

trees.story:
San Diego Magazine went looking for the oldest tree in the city in 2020 and came back with this cypress, then about 128 years old. It is one of the trees Kate Sessions planted under the deal she struck in 1892: the city leased her park land at Sixth and Upas, and in exchange she put a hundred trees a year into Balboa Park. This is among the oldest of her plantings still standing.

The species makes it stranger than the date does. Cupressus guadalupensis grows wild in exactly one place on earth, Isla Guadalupe off Baja California, where feral goats have long been the main threat to what is left of the groves. A large mainland specimen of a tree that rare, on a public lawn beside a chess club, is an odd survival.

Both the Natural History Museum's own account of Sessions and San Diego Magazine name the species, the tree and the spot, and both describe it as enormously tall. Neither publishes a girth or a height, which is the frustrating part of a tree everyone agrees is remarkable. If you can measure it, we will take the number.

A hundred and thirty years is not old in most of the places this site covers. In a city that had to plant its own shade, it is close to the beginning.
trees.how_to_recognise: A very tall cypress on the Sixth Avenue frontage of the park, standing beside the chess and horseshoe club building at 2225 Sixth Avenue.
trees.access: Free, in the open park along Balboa Park's Sixth Avenue frontage, beside the public chess and horseshoe club building.
trees.transport: On the Sixth Avenue side of Balboa Park; served by MTS bus route 3, about a 5 to 10 minute walk from the Cabrillo Bridge / Balboa Park west entrance area.
trees.notes: San Diego Magazine gave approximately 128 years as of 2020; the band here is kept broad rather than sharpened to a single figure. Species string set to the Cupressus form to match the rest of the corpus (Hesperocyparis guadalupensis is the same tree). Coordinates are an estimate of the Sixth Avenue / Ivy Street area by the chess and horseshoe clubs rather than a sourced tree-level position. sandiegoreader.com returned HTTP 403 on every fetch route and is a blocklist candidate.

trees.name: The Kauri by the Mingei Museum

location.address: Beside the Mingei International Museum (House of Charm), Plaza de Panama, Balboa Park, San Diego, CA

trees.story:
There is a New Zealand kauri on the Plaza de Panama and almost nothing about it is written down. Agathis australis is barely grown anywhere in Southern California, which is what makes a mature one standing beside the House of Charm worth crossing the park for, whatever its size turns out to be. The record that confirms it is a single geotagged, photographed observation made in July 2016, still the only record of the species anywhere near San Diego on that platform.

Local pieces have described what is almost certainly this same tree, one of them calling it possibly the most valuable plant in the park, and quoting a height and a rough planting decade. None of those pages could be read directly, so none of their numbers are repeated here. This entry carries no age and no height rather than a figure nobody has checked.

What is left is the tree itself, and it does not look like its neighbours. Kauri grow a straight grey column of a trunk and hold the crown right at the top of it, which reads oddly on a plaza planted with spreading subtropicals.

If you know when it went in, or how tall it is now, tell us. Somebody in San Diego knows, and it is not written down anywhere we can reach.
verified_sources: https://www.sandiegoreader.com/news/2025/nov/10/balboa-park-has-more-than-these-ten-trees/ (Balboa Park horticulturist's estimate of about 65 feet, an estimate not a survey)
trees.access: Free, in the open plaza outside the Mingei International Museum. No admission needed to see the tree itself; the museum charges for entry to its galleries.
trees.transport: Central Balboa Park, on the Plaza de Panama; served by MTS bus route 7 to the Prado, about a 10 minute walk.
trees.notes: Existence, species and position confirmed from a geotagged, photographed iNaturalist observation (id 342689280, 2016-07-09, 32.7313561/-117.1511082), the only Agathis australis record near San Diego on that platform. The second source listed by the verify pass (sandiegoreader.com) returned HTTP 403 on every fetch route and was dropped rather than cited unread, so this ships single-sourced. Its reported height (~65ft, or 52ft measured 1994) and a late-1930s/early-1940s planting estimate came only from search summaries and are deliberately not recorded. sandiegoreader.com and pacifichorticulture.org are blocklist candidates.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by a straight grey column of a trunk holding its crown right at the top, unlike the spreading subtropicals around it. It stands beside the Mingei International Museum on the Plaza de Panama.

trees.name: The Twisted Tea Tree of Marston House

location.address: Marston House Museum grounds, 3525 Seventh Avenue, Balboa Park, San Diego, CA 92103

trees.access: Free to view on the Marston House Museum grounds (part of Balboa Park); the house museum itself charges admission but the garden path this tree stands on is on the museum's public grounds
trees.transport: Balboa Park, northwest corner at Seventh Avenue and Upas Street; bus routes serve Sixth/Seventh Avenue, roughly 10-15 minute walk from central Balboa Park
trees.story:
This tree grows sideways. Its trunks run out almost level with the ground, and where a limb comes down far enough to touch the soil it sometimes puts down roots and carries on. The result, on the grounds of Marston House in Balboa Park, is a low, gnarled tangle that visitors compare to something out of a fantasy novel. Somebody has called it Gandalf. It is not the only name it has been given.

It is an Australian tea tree, and it earns its place here by shape rather than size. Nothing about it is tall. Everything about it is twisted.

The park ranger Kim Duclo says it was likely planted around 1906 by Kate Sessions, the horticulturist remembered as Balboa Park's godmother, the same woman whose last nursery left the tipu tree in Pacific Beach. That would make it about 120 years old. It is one person's informed guess rather than a record, and it is the only date anyone has offered. What is documented is that a professional survey of the Marston garden in 1989 listed Australian tea tree among its plants, though it does not say which specimen.

It stands on the paved walkway just past the entrance to the Marston House grounds, at the park's northwest corner near Seventh Avenue and Upas Street. The garden is free to walk; the house charges for tours inside.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the low, twisting trunks that run almost flat along the ground, some rooting where they touch. It stands beside the paved walkway just past the entrance to the Marston House grounds.

trees.name: The Moreton Bay Fig of Palm Canyon

location.address: Palm Canyon footbridge, near Alcazar Garden, Balboa Park, San Diego, CA 92101

verified_sources: https://www.sandiegoreader.com/news/2025/nov/10/balboa-park-has-more-than-these-ten-trees/ (the fig stands at the steps from the wooden bridge into Palm Canyon)
trees.access: Free; stands beside a public footbridge and steps into Palm Canyon, part of Balboa Park
trees.transport: Central Balboa Park, a short walk south of the Alcazar Garden and west of the Organ Pavilion; served by Balboa Park's free tram and multiple bus routes
trees.story:
The roots of this fig do not stay underground. They pour over the edge of Palm Canyon and run down the slope in great ridged buttresses, and one landscape history of the park compares them to flying buttresses. That is the reason to come, and the reason photographers and wedding parties climb down into the canyon below it.

It is a Moreton Bay fig, and not the famous one. Balboa Park's best-known fig, planted in 1915, stands by the Natural History Museum. This is a separate, younger tree over Palm Canyon, planted around the mid 1930s by one account, or in the 1930s or 1940s by another, which puts it at roughly ninety years.

It has had the better part of a century on the lip of this canyon, and it has used the time to go over the side. The trunk is the anchor. The roots are the show.

The best view is from the wooden footbridge that crosses Palm Canyon from near the Alcazar Garden toward the Organ Pavilion. The pin is an estimate for that stretch of canyon rather than a fix on the trunk, so start at the bridge and look over the side. It is free, open parkland.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the massive buttress roots spilling over the canyon edge and running down the slope. It stands beside the wooden footbridge over Palm Canyon, between the Alcazar Garden and the Organ Pavilion.

location_site.name: Palm Canyon wooden footbridge and the steps down into Palm Canyon

trees.name: The Florence Hotel Moreton Bay Fig

location.address: Grape Street between Third and Fourth Avenues (beside 1927 Fourth Avenue), Bankers Hill, San Diego

trees.access: View from the public sidewalks of Grape Street and Fourth Avenue. The tree stands on a privately owned lot (long a parking lot) behind the Wet Stone cafe, so look from the sidewalk; a sign in front of it names it. Free.
trees.transport: Bus routes on Fourth/Fifth Avenues in Bankers Hill; about a 10 minute walk from the Balboa Park Laurel Street entrance.
trees.recognise: The huge fig on the Grape Street corner of the old Florence Hotel block, with a sign at its foot reading Florence Hotel Moreton Bay Fig Tree.
trees.verify_notes: Last vestige of the Florence Hotel (opened 1884 per Reader 2008; 1893 per Reader 1991; torn down 1948-1950, block became a parking lot). Reader 1991: planted 1895 as part of the hotel garden; City of San Diego Historical Site No. 53 since 1971; by 1991 the owner had neglected it, trunk carved with initials, a section blackened by an attempt at torching; an arborist was hired and a deed restriction required, city staff called it 'the single most protected tree in town'; one of only three mature local Ficus macrophylla then (the others in Balboa Park at Sixth and Laurel and behind the Natural History Museum); arborist Bill Nelson thought it had only 20 to 30 years left, others said 100. Reader 2008: a sign in front says 'Florence Hotel Moreton Bay Fig Tree, 1877' (131 years then); writer stood under it, 'ginormous', spreads over the lot. AGE CONFLICT: 1877 (sign, 2008) vs 1895 (Reader 1991, city landmark record); hotel itself opened 1884 so 1877 predates it; range 130 to 150 years covers both. Alive: iNaturalist observation 328436636, 2025-11-26, GPS accuracy 3 m at 32.72607,-117.16119, Ficus macrophylla, place guess 'Grape St' (photo licence CC BY-NC, not usable); lifecheck.py RECENT. A second iNat Ficus macrophylla at 32.7254,-117.1593 (obs 76762994, 2021) is a different tree, the Balboa Park fig near Sixth and Laurel (about 190 m east). Pin: confirmed from the 3 m GPS fix. Not verified: the 2020-2025 redevelopment of the Fenton Bankers Hill site (carriage house 2004 Fourth Ave, 328 Grape St); the fig was standing Nov 2025 but check it is still reachable from the sidewalk. Private lot: ships as view-only with the pin on the viewing place. One source for the landmark status (San Diego Reader 1991), flagged. No girth or height published.
trees.how_to_recognise: The huge fig spreading over the old Florence Hotel lot on the Grape Street side, with a sign at its foot reading Florence Hotel Moreton Bay Fig Tree.
trees.story:
A hotel stood here once, and this fig is what is left of it. The Florence Hotel opened in Bankers Hill in the 1880s or 1890s, depending on the account, and was torn down around 1948 to 1950. The block became a parking lot, and the fig from the hotel garden stayed. A sign at its foot says 1877, which would make the tree older than the hotel. The San Diego Reader, writing in 1991, gave 1895, the date the city's landmark record uses. Somewhere between 130 and 150 years, then.

The city made it Historical Site No. 53 in 1971, and being a landmark did not keep it safe. By 1991 initials had been carved into its trunk and part of it was blackened where someone had tried to set it alight. An arborist was brought in, a deed restriction followed, and city staff called it the single most protected tree in town. One arborist that year gave it twenty or thirty more years. It was still standing, and still spreading over the lot, in November 2025.

The fig is on private ground, so this is one to look at from the sidewalk on Grape Street or Fourth Avenue. The land around it has been redeveloped in recent years and we have not seen how that changed the view from the street; tell us if it has. Balboa Park's Laurel Street entrance is about ten minutes' walk away.

trees.name: The Kensington Hoop Pine

location.address: Kensington Library Park, 4121 Adams Avenue, San Diego

trees.access: Free, open public park lawn around the Normal Heights-Kensington library (library opening hours apply inside only).
trees.transport: Bus along Adams Avenue (Kensington); roughly a 15 minute drive or bus ride from Balboa Park.
trees.recognise: The very tall conifer on the corner of the park, strung with lights every December; four older Canary Island pines flank the former pond site.
trees.verify_notes: Heritage Grove: the City of San Diego Community Forest Advisory Board voted unanimously on 14 January 2009 to designate the Kensington library park trees as a Heritage Grove and Landmark trees (SOHO 2009 article; SOHO March-April 2023 newsletter via obrag.org repeats it). Kensington Park was subdivided in 1910 (lot sales opened 25 Nov 1910); SOHO 2023: nine original trees remain in the park around the library, planted 1910 by the developers: Canary Island pines, Canary Island palms, a deodar cedar, a Catalina Island cherry and a hoop pine. SOHO 2009: historic 1913 images show the hoop pine 'in the same position that it occupies today'; four Canary Island pines (Pinus canariensis), two each side of the former goldfish pond, also still stand. 1962 library expansion removed some originals; architect Richard Lareau left roofline cutouts for two Canary Island pines. SOHO 2023 describes the hoop pine as 'a very tall tree on the corner of the park', lit every December; KPBS lists the annual Kensington Park tree lighting (Friday 24 Nov 2023, 4121 Adams Ave) but does not name the species. Age basis: 1913 photograph plus 1910 subdivision; no planting year for this specimen stated, so age is 'over a century' (110 to 116). The two SOHO pages are one organisation, the official designation is the second leg. No girth or height published. Pin: park-level, no tree coordinate found (no iNaturalist, OSM tree node or Commons geotag for it); small named site, approximate. Not checked: which exact corner (Terrace Drive end vs Adams Avenue end); the listed 'tall hoop pine' may not be the lit tree in every year. Alive: SOHO 2023 describes the trees as surviving; no dated photograph in hand.
trees.how_to_recognise: The very tall conifer on a corner of the small park around the Kensington library; four Canary Island pines stand two on each side of the former pond site.
trees.story:
When Kensington was laid out as a new subdivision in 1910, its developers planted a park around what is now the neighbourhood library. Nine of those first trees are still here, and a photograph from 1913 already shows this hoop pine in the same spot it stands in today. Hoop pine is an Araucaria from the rainforests of eastern Australia, and here it has grown into the very tall tree on the corner of the park.

It has had company from the start: four Canary Island pines, two on each side of the old goldfish pond, along with Canary Island palms, a deodar cedar and a Catalina Island cherry. When the library was enlarged in 1962 some of the original trees were lost, and the architect, Richard Lareau, cut openings in the roofline so that two of the Canary Island pines could stay. In 2009 the City's Community Forest Advisory Board voted unanimously to make the whole group a Heritage Grove.

Every December the neighbourhood holds a tree lighting in the park, and the preservation group SOHO describes the tall hoop pine as the tree that is lit. We could not pin the trunk itself, so the map point marks the park; a reader's photograph from beside it would settle which corner. The park is free and open, and only the library keeps opening hours.

trees.name: The Torrey Pine at Coronado Library

location.address: Coronado Public Library, 640 Orange Ave, Coronado, CA

official_register.name: City of Coronado Heritage Trees list (as reproduced by Coronado Times, 2022)

trees.access: Free. Stands near the front entrance of the Coronado Public Library, viewable from the public walkway at any time.
trees.transport: Coronado sits across the bay from downtown San Diego (ferry from the Broadway Pier to the Ferry Landing, or bus over the Coronado Bridge; roughly 15 to 30 minutes, not checked against a timetable). Library is on Orange Avenue, downtown Coronado.
trees.recognise: The Torrey pine beside the library's front entrance, with the two taller Norfolk Island pines flanking the doors.
trees.verify_notes: Day-trip edge: this is Coronado, a separate city across the bay; label it as Coronado. The city's own Heritage Tree list is the naming body (15 trees); public-space ones only delivered, private-yard ones kept as leads. The city PDF itself 403s to curl and WebFetch; the Coronado Times article reproduces the list and credits the City, and was read via a web.archive.org copy (live page 403s). City Heritage Tree Serial 002, designated 3 April 2008. City text: typical of the Torreys planted about a century ago in a city-wide programme under Parks Superintendent Louis C. Bandel, 'assisted by Kate Sessions'; Coronado Torreys grow to more than 50 ft. Alive: iNaturalist observations at the library on 2017-12-17 (5 m accuracy) and 2024-10-25 (9 m), both casual grade, coordinates 32.69116,-117.17700 and 32.69125,-117.17699; the Heritage Tree label is read from the city text, not the iNat species ID. Pin is a GPS fix at the library entrance but two other conifers stand there, so the Torrey is picked by species in the iNat records. One city source plus two iNat fixes: flagged one source. Tree 001 (Palm Park) is the city's Official Tree since 2006. Kate Sessions link is only the City's wording, do not enlarge it.
trees.story:
Coronado keeps an official list of fifteen heritage trees, and the Torrey pine outside its public library is serial 002 on it. The city designated it on 3 April 2008, and its own description of the tree is really a description of a whole town's planting.

About a century ago, Coronado planted Torrey pines in a city-wide programme under Louis C. Bandel, its Parks Superintendent, 'assisted by Kate Sessions' in the city's own words. This tree is called typical of those plantings. Coronado's Torreys, the city adds, grow to more than 50 feet. No measurement has been published for this one, and the century is the city's round figure rather than a recorded planting date.

What makes the library a good place to start is the company. The library entrance carries three heritage conifers at once. This Torrey pine stands near the front doors, and the two taller Norfolk Island pines planted in 1909 for the opening of the Spreckels Library flank them.

Coronado is its own city, across the bay from downtown San Diego, so treat it as a short day trip. The ferry from the Broadway Pier or a bus over the Coronado Bridge gets you here in roughly 15 to 30 minutes; check the timetable. The library is on Orange Avenue in the middle of town, and the tree is free to see from the public walkway at any hour.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the Torrey pine by the library's front entrance, shorter than the two Norfolk Island pines that flank the doors. It stands outside Coronado Public Library on Orange Avenue.

trees.name: The 1909 Library Pines of Coronado

location.address: Coronado Public Library, 640 Orange Ave, Coronado, CA

official_register.name: City of Coronado Heritage Trees list (as reproduced by Coronado Times, 2022)

trees.access: Free. Two trees either side of the library's main entrance, viewable from the public walkway at any time.
trees.transport: Coronado sits across the bay from downtown San Diego (ferry from the Broadway Pier to the Ferry Landing, or bus over the Coronado Bridge; roughly 15 to 30 minutes, not checked against a timetable). Library is on Orange Avenue, downtown Coronado.
trees.recognise: The matched pair of tall Norfolk Island pines on either side of the library's main entrance.
trees.verify_notes: Day-trip edge: this is Coronado, a separate city across the bay; label it as Coronado. The city's own Heritage Tree list is the naming body (15 trees); public-space ones only delivered, private-yard ones kept as leads. The city PDF itself 403s to curl and WebFetch; the Coronado Times article reproduces the list and credits the City, and was read via a web.archive.org copy (live page 403s). City Heritage Tree Serials 012 and 013 (folded into one entry, a matched pair at one spot), both designated 6 Oct 2016, both 'planted in 1909 with the opening of the Spreckels Library'; Coronado Historical Association blog independently ties the two Norfolk pines on the library grounds to 1909 (it names no planter). City text says the species reaches about 100 ft at maturity (no measured height for these). Alive: one iNaturalist observation of a Norfolk Island pine at the library, 2020-07-22, 32.69099,-117.17720 (10 m accuracy, casual). Pin is the library entrance, approximate; use the small-site rule. Photo candidate: that iNat photo is CC BY-NC, not usable.
trees.story:
These two Norfolk Island pines went into the ground the year the library they guard opened its doors. That was 1909, and the library was the new Spreckels Library. More than a century later they still stand either side of its main entrance.

Two sources date them independently. The City of Coronado's Heritage Tree list, which designated both on 6 October 2016 as serials 012 and 013, says they were planted with the library's opening. The Coronado Historical Association ties the pair on the library grounds to 1909 as well, without naming who planted them. That makes them about 117 years old, a firmer date than the round century the city gives its Torrey pines.

The city notes that the species reaches about 100 feet at maturity. Nobody has published a measured height for these two, so that figure describes the species rather than this pair.

You see them together from one spot on the walkway. Near the same entrance stands a Torrey pine, another of the city's fifteen heritage trees, so the library gives you three in one stop.

Coronado is a separate city across the bay from downtown San Diego. Take the ferry from the Broadway Pier or a bus over the Coronado Bridge, roughly 15 to 30 minutes; check the timetable. The library is on Orange Avenue, and both pines are free to see from the public walkway at any time.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the matched pair of tall Norfolk Island pines, one on each side of the library's main entrance. They stand at the front of Coronado Public Library on Orange Avenue.

trees.story:
Coronado's Christmas tree has been the same living pine since 1936. That year Louis C. Bandel, the city's Parks Superintendent, moved this Norfolk Island pine to Rotary Plaza with money from the town's Rotarians, and in the city's words it has served as Coronado's living Christmas tree ever since. Each December it is lit again.

The City of Coronado put it on its Heritage Tree list on 3 April 2008, as serial 003. The transplant is the only date anyone has. It was moved here, not planted here, so it had already been growing somewhere else, for how long nobody recorded. About 90 years is therefore a floor, not an estimate, and the true figure is higher by however long it grew somewhere else first.

One honest caution. The most recent dated sighting we could find is a visitor's record from November 2021, and the city's description from 2022 still speaks of the Christmas tree role as ongoing. We have no reason to think it has gone, but if you visit, tell us it is still standing.

Coronado is a separate city across the bay from downtown San Diego, a short day trip by the ferry from the Broadway Pier or a bus over the Coronado Bridge, roughly 15 to 30 minutes; check the timetable. The plaza sits off Orange Avenue near Olive Avenue, and the tree is free to see at any hour. Online maps label it Rotary Park.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the single tall Norfolk Island pine that Coronado dresses as its Christmas tree each December. It stands in Rotary Plaza, off Orange Avenue near Olive Avenue.

trees.story:
This Torrey pine has a park almost to itself, and the park has a sailor's name. Cronan Park is a small triangle of public ground at Sixth Street and Pomona Avenue, and the City of Coronado's heritage list says the tree dominates it, a grand Torrey in the same mould as the city's official tree in Palm Park and the one outside the library.

The name belongs to William Cronan, a Medal of Honor recipient who served as a bosun's mate aboard the USS Bennington when the ship exploded in San Diego harbour in 1905.

The city put the pine on its Heritage Tree list on 5 May 2011, as serial 004. Its age is the soft part. The city says Coronado's Torreys were planted about a century ago, but that sentence is written for the library tree, and this one is only called similar. Over a century is a fair reading, and nobody has published a planting year or a measurement for it.

Coronado is a separate city across the bay from downtown San Diego, a short day trip by the ferry from the Broadway Pier or a bus over the Coronado Bridge, roughly 15 to 30 minutes; check the timetable. The pin here is a visitor's GPS fix on the tree itself. It is free to see at any hour.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big Torrey pine that dominates the small triangular park. It stands at the corner of Sixth Street and Pomona Avenue in Coronado.

trees.story:
Coronado has an official tree, and it is not a species but a single Torrey pine in Palm Park. The City Council recognised it as the city's Official Tree in 2006, and on 3 April 2008 it became serial 001, the first of fifteen on Coronado's Heritage Tree list.

The city's account says it was planted early in the twentieth century under the supervision of Louis C. Bandel, who served as Parks Superintendent for forty years. Bandel's name runs through the list. The Torrey outside the library came from his city-wide planting programme, and in 1936 he moved the pine that is now Coronado's Christmas tree into Rotary Plaza. No planting year and no measurement have been published, so over a century is the honest figure.

One caution on finding it. The city places Palm Park at Palm Avenue and Third Street, and a visitor's GPS record from January 2025 puts a Torrey pine inside the park. It is the only Torrey in the visitor records for the park, which makes it very likely the official tree, but the record is not tied to the heritage label, so our pin is marked approximate.

Coronado is a separate city across the bay from downtown San Diego. The ferry from the Broadway Pier takes roughly 15 to 30 minutes (check the timetable), and the park is a short walk from where it lands. It is free and open to walk through.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the Torrey pine in Palm Park, the one the City Council named Coronado's Official Tree. It stands in the park at Palm Avenue and Third Street, near the Ferry Landing.
